newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN says only four Hutu returnees killed in Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: UN says only four Hutu returnees killed in Rwanda.

text.p: The U.N. Commissioner for Human Rights said on Monday that just four Hutu refugees among 550,000 who returned to Rwanda from eastern Zaire last month were killed since they got back and another 162 had been arrested.

The commissioner, Jose Ayala-Lasso, also said after returning from a trip to Rwanda that he had no time on this occasion to visit neighbouring Burundi where at least 300 Burundian Hutus have been massacred since returning home.

"I didn't go on this occasion to Burundi, simply due to time constraints," he told a news briefing. Latest field information about Hutu returnees in war-ravaged Burundi, where there are only five U.N. human rights monitors, were not yet available.

In Burundi, where 150,000 people have died in three years of war between the almost exclusively Tutsi army and Hutu rebels, the United Nations said last month 298 Hutu returnees were massacred in the northwestern Cibitoke warzone in October.

In Rwanda, where more than half a million Tutsis and Hutu moderates died in a Hutu-led genocide in 1994 after which a Tutsi-dominated army swept to power, Ayala-Lasso said four returnees and two associates were killed after fleeing a Tutsi rebellion in east Zaire.
Since the mass influx, U.N. human rights observers reported the killings of four genocide survivors and two associates by Hutu returnees in three separate incidents, he added.
Ayala-Laso said he had assurances from Rwandan leaders to prevent ethnic tensions from rising. "I hope we won't have an increased number of people killed. Tensions are there," he said.
The Rwandan returnees included 4,331 members of the former extremist Hutu army, which played a key role in the genocide. Among them, 12 had been arrested, the U.N. said.
Rwanda is Africa's most crowded country and a centuries-old struggle for farmland is at the root of much of the conflict between majority Hutus and minority Tutsis.

Diplomats fear arrests may rise as Hutu returnees try to claim back property taken over by Tutsis -- some 800,000 of whom recently returned from exile after fleeing earlier bouts of conflict, almost a one-to-one replacement of the genocide dead.
